writing.exampleCaption: `?` returns early on the error case, keeping the happy path flat.
writing.explanation:
Pattern matching and the `?` operator keep both cases explicit without null, sentinel values, or exceptions. Reach for `Option` when absence is normal and expected, and `Result` when the caller needs to know why something did not work.

Ask what the caller needs to know when there is no value. If a search simply finds nothing, `Option<T>` describes the two normal outcomes: `Some(item)` or `None`. If a parser fails, `Result<T, E>` describes success plus a reason for failure. Neither type is a disguised boolean. They carry the successful value, and `Result` preserves information needed to explain or recover from the error.

Use `match` when both outcomes deserve visible behavior. `if let Some(item) = lookup()` is compact when you only care about the present case. `map` transforms a value inside `Some` or `Ok` without inventing a value for the other case. `unwrap_or` supplies a deliberate default; use it only when the default is genuinely correct. `?` can return early for an absent `Option` or an error `Result` when the surrounding function has the appropriate return type. A function returning `Result` cannot use `?` on an `Option` without explicitly choosing what error absence means.

For the exercise, make `find(id)` return `Option<Item>` because missing data is expected. Make `parse_id(raw)` return `Result<u32, ParseIntError>` because malformed input has a reason. Combine them in a caller: parse first, then look up, and show distinct messages for malformed and unknown IDs. Avoid `unwrap()` on both paths; it collapses two normal situations into a panic. Good types help the caller write a useful interface.

`Option<T>` answers whether a value is present. `Some(T)` carries the value; `None` means absence. `Result<T, E>` answers whether an operation succeeded. `Ok(T)` carries success; `Err(E)` carries a reason for failure. They are different questions. A search that finds no item may return `None`; a failed file read needs an error that explains what went wrong. Choosing the right type tells callers what decision to make.

Take a lookup function and test three cases: item found, item missing, and storage unavailable. If the last case is possible, a single `Option` cannot communicate it well; consider `Result<Option<T>, E>`. Unwrap only when you have proved the variant or intentionally want to crash on an invariant violation. Prefer `match`, `if let`, or combinators when they keep both paths visible. Ask what information a caller needs at the boundary, then choose the return type.
